content: Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) represent a diverse group of illnesses caused by bacterial, viral, or other pathogens. Procalcitonin (PCT), a biomarker found in the blood, has gained attention as a tool to guide decisions regarding antibiotic therapy. This approach, known as PCT-guided antibiotic therapy, has been evaluated in numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) across various clinical settings, including primary care, emergency departments, hospital wards, and intensive care units. However, the impact of PCT-guided therapy on clinical outcomes remains uncertain. This study is an updated Cochrane review and meta-analysis, originally published in 2012, aimed at assessing the safety and efficacy of PCT-guided antibiotic use in ARIs. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of using procalcitonin to guide the initiation and discontinuation of antibiotics in patients with ARIs of varying severity and across different clinical environments. To identify relevant trials, databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase were searched in February 2017. Additionally, ClinicalTrials.gov was reviewed in April 2017 to identify ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria were RCTs involving adult patients with ARIs who received antibiotics based on either a PCT-guided algorithm or standard care. Trials focusing exclusively on children or using procalcitonin for purposes other than guiding antibiotic therapy were excluded. Two independent teams of reviewers assessed the methodology and extracted data from the included studies. The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and treatment failure within 30 days, with definitions standardized across trials. Secondary outcomes included antibiotic use, antibiotic-related side effects, and length of hospital stay. Statistical analyses were performed using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression models, adjusting for factors such as age, gender, and clinical diagnosis. Sensitivity analyses were conducted based on clinical setting and type of ARI. The meta-analysis included individual participant data from 26 RCTs, encompassing 6708 participants, out of 32 eligible trials. Four trials did not provide individual participant data, and two trials were excluded as they did not involve confirmed ARIs. The quality of evidence, as assessed by GRADE, was high for mortality and antibiotic exposure outcomes, and moderate for treatment failure and antibiotic-related side effects. For the primary outcomes, mortality was significantly lower in the PCT-guided group, with 286 deaths among 3336 participants (8.6%) compared to 336 deaths among 3372 controls (10.0%). This corresponded to an adjusted odds ratio (OR) of 0.83 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 0.99, P = 0.037). Mortality could not be reliably assessed in primary care settings due to the low number of deaths. Treatment failure rates were not significantly different between the PCT-guided group (23.0%) and the control group (24.9%), with an adjusted OR of 0.90 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.01, P = 0.068). Subgroup analyses by clinical setting and type of ARI showed consistent results, with no evidence of effect modification. For the secondary outcomes, PCT guidance was associated with a significant reduction in antibiotic exposure, with a mean duration of 5.7 days in the PCT group compared to 8.1 days in the control group (mean difference -2.4 days, 95% CI -2.71 to -2.15, P < 0.001). The risk of antibiotic-related side effects was also lower in the PCT group (16.3%) compared to controls (22.1%), with an adjusted OR of 0.68 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.82, P < 0.001). Lengths of hospital stay and intensive care unit stay were similar between the two groups. An aggregate data analysis of all 32 eligible trials yielded comparable results. In conclusion, this updated meta-analysis, which included data from 12 countries, demonstrates that PCT-guided antibiotic therapy in ARIs is associated with reduced mortality, decreased antibiotic use, and a lower risk of antibiotic-related side effects. These findings were consistent across different clinical settings and types of ARIs, supporting the use of procalcitonin as a tool for antibiotic stewardship in ARIs. Further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings in immunosuppressed patients and those with non-respiratory infections.
